The amount of pressure drop in the center and the rate at which it increases outwards gives the intensity of the cyclones and the strength of winds.

The methodology is based on computing the Hurricane return period by NOAA. Cyclone return periods are the frequency at which a certain cyclone intensity can be expected within a given distance of a given location within a specified buffer zone around the district(we have considered 50 nm as a buffer zone).

Extremely severe cyclone Fani hit the Odisha coast in Puri early morning of 3 May 2019 with wind speed around 175 km/h. According to the Indian Meteorological Department, in the past 126 years (1891-2017) only 14 severe tropical cyclones have formed in April over the BoB. Out of those, only one storm crossed the Indian mainland. Cyclone Fani became the second storm formed in April that crossed the mainland. The last severe cyclone Nargis in 2008 devastated Myanmar. After landfall, cyclone Fani moved towards the northeast at the same speed for some time and then weakened gradually. The track of the cyclone is shown in Figure 1. Figure 2 shows a glimpse of destruction as it pounded Odisha and West Bengal on the day of landfall on 3 May 2019. The cyclone was categorized as an extremely severe cyclone (Source: IMD).

The average air temperature before the cyclone over the ocean was 28.43 ºC during 2019 and 27\.80 ºC in 2018, the temperature in 2019 was higher over the ocean. Yet the average temperature over land was 29.83 ºC during 2019 and 30.21 ºC during 2018.
The sea temperature was found to rise by 2 o C before the cyclone all along the coastal line and over the BoB and Andaman sea.

Negative Omega values are observed on 29 April over the Indian Ocean and the eastern parts of India. During 1 – 3 May 2019, Omega at 850 hPa pressure level was not much negative due to its faster linear motion towards the coasts of Odisha.

Changes in TCO, especially the decline of TCO is observed from 28 April 2019. One day before the landfall, it reduced approximately 17% over Boxes 1 and 2, 10 % over Box 3, and about 7\.53% over Box 4. Low TCO was observed even on 4 May 2019.

Over Boxes 1, 2, and 3, higher CO in the middle and upper troposphere was observed before the cyclone but as the cyclone reached close to the coastal region, CO concentration declined on 2 and 3 May 2019 in the middle troposphere.

On 2 May 2019, low CO concentration was observed on 2 May 2019 around 20 (higher altitude) and 925 (close to the surface) hPa in troposphere. On 3 May 2019 a rise in CO concentrations was observed at the pressure levels 20-100 hPa and on 4 May 2019 rise in CO concentration was observed at pressure levels 150 – 925 hPa.

A small rise in AOD values over Box 1 during 23 to 29 April was observed due to strong cyclonic winds. Once the cyclone moved further over the land towards north-eastern parts after the landfall, AOD declined which could be due to scavenging effect due to precipitation associated with the cyclone.

The contrast in ocean temperature during 2019 could be a favorable condition in the formation of the cyclone Fani.

The air temperature contrast between land-ocean temperature in 2019 was higher that may have played a favorable role in the formation of cyclone Fani along with other meteorological conditions. The air temperature was higher over the land (blue line) and the ocean (red line) during April and May 2019. excerpts: Unfortunately, the data collected by TBRGs is famously unreliable, being affected by a multitude of errors and typically underestimating rainfall by 5%–40% (Sypka, 2019 ).
In general, the mechanical limitations of modern TBRGs result in a nonlinear underestimation of rainfall, an error between 2% and 30% (Shedekar _et al_ ., 2016 ).
However, these errors can be minor compared to the potential 75% underestimation of rainfall during stormy conditions due to undercatch (Neff, 1977 ).

This underestimation decreases with increasing rain gauge resolution and increases with increasing rainfall intensity; above rainfall intensities of 30–50mmh −1 the reliability of TBRGs diminishes rapidly due to the saturation effect (Duchon and Biddle, 2010 ; Tapiador _et al_ ., 2012 ).

Additionally, due to the bucket's volume dictating the minimum recording volume, information about the intermittency and intensity distribution of low rainfall rates is typically very poor (Fankhauser, 1997 ).

For more modern TBRGs, wind-induced undercatch generally reduces rainfall estimation by 5%–46%, dependent on the gauge design, set-up and the ambient conditions (Duchon and Essenberg, 2001 ; Mekonnen _et al_ ., 2015 ; Pollock _et al_ ., 2018 ).

Wind-induced undercatch results from the airflow around the TBRG being deformed by the presence of the gauge itself, and hence is unavoidable (see Figure 5 , Constantinescu _et al_ ., 2007 ). The deformation alters the trajectories of the raindrops, deviating them away from the collector (Cauteruccio _et al_ ., 2020 ).

Wind-induced undercatch extent is also influenced by the following: windspeed, the extent of undercatch for an unshielded rain gauge has been shown to increase by approximately 1%–2.2% for each mph increase in windspeed (Bratzev, 1963 ; Larson, 1971 ; Larson and Peck, 1974 ); wind turbulence, as precipitation behaves differently in uniform and fluctuating wind conditions (Cauteruccio, 2020 ); and the drop size distribution (DSD) of the rain, as trajectories of smaller droplets are affected more by wind than larger ones (Nešpor and Sevruk, 1999 ).

In terms of counting errors, the primary systematic errors are typically a result of a gauge's mechanical limitations or poor installation (Habib _et al_ ., 2001 ; La Barbera _et al_ ., 2002 ). Refinement of the gauge's mechanisms and adherence to installation best practices can help to mitigate such errors. Due to technological limitations, however, these errors cannot be fully eliminated. Hence, the application of a gauge-specific empirical calibration function is also recommended (Tapiador _et al_ ., 2012 ).

Undercatch cannot be eliminated, and network heterogeneity is inevitable. Therefore, correction factors (CFs) are required to estimate the actual volume of rainfall at the gauge. This concept is not a novel one: since the 1980s, various attempts have been made to develop an effective CF for TBRGs.

While existing CFs have been demonstrated to be successful in their improvement of precipitation data (Feng _et al_ ., 2024 ), further research is still required in this area, with no singular CF being widely applied or accepted, and existing CFs resulting in significantly different rainfall estimations (Ehsani and Behrangi, 2022 ).

Both catching and counting errors can be random or systematic. Random errors encompass factors such as human error and equipment failure; hence, they are typically unpredictable, sudden and difficult to correct for. Data quality control or co-located gauges are therefore the optimum strategy for handling such errors (Ciach, 2003 ; Blenkinsop _et al_ ., 2016 ).

Improvements in installation practices have evolved alongside improved gauge design. It has been demonstrated that instrumentation height influences undercatch extent (Pollock _et al_ ., 2018 ), with higher TBRGs experiencing stronger effects from wind (Mekonnen _et al_ ., 2015 ). Consequently, TBRG's in the United Kingdom are now installed at ground level, thus reducing wind exposure and creating measurement consistency across the network (Muchan and Dixon, 2019 ). However, this practice is not necessarily replicated in other countries, and does increase the risk of debris being blown into the orifice and splash-in (Sieck _et al_ ., 2007 ).

Refinement of the gauge's mechanisms and adherence to installation best practices can help to mitigate such errors. Due to technological limitations, however, these errors cannot be fully eliminated. Hence, the application of a gauge-specific empirical calibration function is also recommended (Tapiador _et al_ ., 2012 ).

Additionally, nowadays greater consideration is typically given to a gauge's siting in terms of its surrounding terrain and its proximity to obstructions (Suri and Azad, 2024 ). The recording of detailed metadata on gauge siting is crucial, both with regards to gauge type and site description, to capture these discrepancies and provide context to measurements.

Undercatch is the most challenging error impacting the reliability of TBRG measurements due to its multifaceted and dynamic nature (Figure 4 , Sieck _et al_ ., 2007 ). Furthermore, undercatch is very location-specific in both extent and causation (Ye _et al_ ., 2004 ; Buisán _et al_ ., 2017 ; Herrnegger _et al_ ., 2018 ).
